description: We are a passionate team of problem-solvers, creators, and space enthusiasts eager to tackle real-world challenges using science, technology, and design. Our team combines a strong interest in space exploration, data analysis, coding, and creative storytelling. We thrive on learning fast, thinking outside the box, and building impactful solutions.
summary: EGIZ is a data-driven Earth-to-planet analog search platform designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It identifies places on Earth that best match lunar south-pole and Martian landing environments by comparing terrain, geology, climate, illumination, and mission-relevant conditions across multiple dimensions. Using NASA and open geospatial datasets, the system ranks candidate regions, quantifies uncertainty, and shows where each analogy breaks down, helping users understand not just the best matches but also the limits of each comparison. This matters because finding strong analog sites is crucial for testing rover operations, habitat planning, geology studies, and mission strategies before sending equipment to the Moon or Mars. EGIZ turns complex planetary and Earth science data into a practical decision tool that supports safer, smarter, and more evidence-based exploration planning.
details:
EGIZ is an interactive platform for finding and evaluating Earth locations that resemble sites on the Moon or Mars. It compares measured terrain and environmental characteristics across candidate regions, ranks potential analogs for different mission goals, and shows uncertainty and the dimensions where each match falls short. Users can explore results on a map, compare candidate sites, review a transparent evidence dossier, and investigate terrain in a 3D Mission Lab with rover-route and operating scenarios.

The project aims to help researchers and mission planners identify useful places on Earth to test exploration technologies and plan field campaigns—while making clear that an analog is not proof of planetary equivalence or site safety. We considered measurement quality, data coverage, uncertainty, mission objectives, and the difference between scientific similarity and practical access.

We built the prototype with TypeScript, Python, and CSS. Its data sources include NASA’s LOLA lunar elevation products, MOLA data in a USGS Mars terrain product, NASA POWER climate data, HiRISE terrain, and NASA SPICE kernels, alongside Earth datasets such as Copernicus DEM. Its creative approach is to combine Earth-wide discovery with explainable, dimension-by-dimension comparisons and explicit “analogy gap” reporting. The prototype is exploratory; scientific review and broader validation remain necessary.
